explain.say: Power stations, cement works and steel plants release carbon dioxide in their exhaust gas. Carbon capture passes this gas through a liquid solvent, often a type called an amine, that soaks up the carbon dioxide.

explain.say: The solvent is then heated, releasing almost pure carbon dioxide, and the solvent is reused. The gas is squeezed until it becomes dense, almost like a liquid, so it is easier to move.

explain.say: Pipelines or ships carry it to a storage site, such as an old gas field under the sea. There it is pumped more than a kilometre down into porous rock, filling the tiny spaces between grains like water in a sponge.

explain.say: A thick layer of solid caprock above traps it, just as such rocks trapped oil and gas for millions of years. Capture uses a lot of energy and is costly, but it can cut emissions from industries with few other options.

faq.a: Most plants pass the exhaust gas through a solvent, such as an amine solution, which chemically grabs carbon dioxide. Heating the solvent later releases the carbon dioxide so the solvent can be reused.

faq.q: Why is captured carbon dioxide compressed?
faq.a: Squeezed to high pressure, carbon dioxide becomes a dense fluid taking up hundreds of times less space, so far more can travel through a pipeline and fit into the rock.

faq.q: Where is captured carbon dioxide stored?
faq.a: Deep underground, usually more than 800 metres down, in porous sandstone or old oil and gas fields, often under the seabed. At that depth the pressure keeps it dense.
asks: How deep is carbon dioxide buried?

faq.q: Could stored carbon dioxide leak out?
faq.a: Sites are chosen with a thick, solid caprock above, the same kind of seal that held oil and gas for millions of years. Over time some carbon dioxide also dissolves in salty water underground or turns into minerals, locking it in further.

faq.q: Does carbon capture solve climate change?
faq.a: It helps, especially for cement, whose chemistry releases carbon dioxide whatever fuel is used. But it is costly, uses energy and catches only part of the gas, so cutting emissions at the source matters most.
asks: Is carbon capture a good idea?

facts: Norway's Sleipner project has stored about one million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year under the North Sea since 1996.
Carbon dioxide stored deep underground is kept in a dense state by the high pressure.

quiz.say: What stops carbon dioxide stored deep underground from rising back to the surface?
quiz.show: Stored carbon dioxide is held down by…

options.show: A layer of solid caprock above it
options.say: A layer of solid caprock above it

quiz.why: A thick, solid caprock seals the porous rock below, just as it once trapped oil and gas.

wrong.1: No man-made lid could cover a whole rock layer; natural caprock does the job.
wrong.2: It is kept dense by pressure deep underground, not frozen.
